headline contribution assesses the validity or mutual agreement of existing faithfulness metrics or tests
harmful or borderline requests where the behavior of interest is refuse vs. comply (e.g. HarmBench, StrongREJECT, WildGuardTest)
free-form continuation or next-text prediction of natural text with no task answer (e.g. Wikipedia continuation, next word)

validates or stress-tests the measuring instrument itself (judge or monitor sanity checks and swaps, answer-leakage baselines, prompt-template robustness, in-distribution checks on edited inputs)
explicitly controls for a named confound that could fake the effect (CoT length, benchmark contamination, conversation context)
tracks the target along an axis (model size, training checkpoints, inference or monitor compute) rather than at a single point

notes: The biggest gap in the seed was a namespace for what analysis papers vary. Coders independently coined three namespaces (factor:, pressure:, stressor:) and coded outcome-only RL three different ways under lever:, so I merged them into one factor: namespace. That namespace shows a sizeable strand (about 10 papers) that studies side effects of training that is not aimed at faithfulness (outcome RL, CoT-length pressure, CoT graders) or model properties (monitor awareness, CoT necessity, controllability) rather than proposing fixes; lever: should stay for interventions aimed at faithfulness. Most coined eval tags were Goodhart and instrument checks: scoring with held-out metrics, monitors or simulators, validating judges and masked inputs, and controlling length, contamination or context confounds. Each is done by only 1 to 5 papers, which suggests evaluation rigor is ad hoc and deserves its own column. The new reveals/object/signal values show that part of the 'faithfulness' literature actually targets reasoning validity, consistency with the model's own stated plan, internal uncertainty, or the honesty of the final output, and often uses references or output agreement rather than the model's decision process; red-team attacks and meta-evaluation of metrics also emerge as distinct contribution types. Metrics are extremely fragmented: about 285 coined names reduce to about 262 after 24 true-synonym merges (Chen et al.'s hint verbalization rate appeared under 7 names, Lanham's early-answering AOC under 3). Only about two dozen metrics are used by more than one paper, and I kept near-twins with different definitions apart: g-mean vs g-mean², conditional hint verbalization vs unconditional cue acknowledgment, per-question vs marginal bias-switch rates, unfaithful-correct over all items vs over correct items. Model names were mostly consistent; the only fixes were Qwen spelling, MoE active-parameter suffixes and thinking-mode aliases, and one tag (metric:verbalization-rate on shenoy2026introspection) needs a manual re-tag because it names a different quantity.
